Paylines vs. "Ways to Win" Slots: How the Math Actually Differs

Published October 18, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Two slots can look almost identical — same five reels, same three rows, same symbols — and still pay out on a fundamentally different basis. One counts a win only when matching symbols land on one of a fixed set of zigzagging lines. The other counts a win whenever matching symbols land anywhere in adjacent reels, regardless of row. That second category shows up under labels like "243 ways to win," "1,024 ways," or "all-ways," and the difference isn't cosmetic — it changes how often you win, how big a typical win tends to be, and how the game's advertised numbers should actually be read.

How a traditional payline slot counts a win

A classic payline slot defines a fixed set of paths across the reel grid in advance — usually drawn as straight lines, zigzags, or V-shapes connecting one symbol position per reel. A common older format is 25 or 30 fixed lines across a five-reel, three-row grid. To win on any given line, the matching symbols have to land in the exact positions that line passes through, starting from the leftmost reel and reading left to right (a handful of games also pay right to left, but that's a less common variant).

This means two spins can land visually similar clusters of matching symbols, and one pays while the other doesn't — if the symbols happen to fall one row off from where an active payline runs, that match simply isn't counted. Players sometimes find this counterintuitive the first time they notice it, because the eye naturally registers "three matching symbols are touching" as a win regardless of which exact line they fall on.

How a "ways to win" slot counts a win instead

A ways-to-win slot throws out the idea of a fixed path entirely. Instead, a win is counted whenever matching symbols appear anywhere in adjacent reels, starting from reel one and moving left to right, regardless of which row each symbol lands in. If reel one has a matching symbol in the top row, reel two has one in the bottom row, and reel three has one in the middle row, that's still a valid win — the specific vertical position of each symbol no longer matters, only that the reels line up in sequence.

The practical effect: a ways-to-win slot pays out far more often on small, partial matches than a payline slot with the same symbols, because it's no longer possible to land a "near miss" where the right symbols touch but fall just outside a scoring line. If the symbols are adjacent across reels, it counts — full stop.

Why 243 and 1,024 are the numbers you keep seeing

The "243 ways" and "1,024 ways" labels aren't marketing flourishes — they're literal counts of every possible left-to-right symbol combination the grid can produce, and they come straight from the grid's dimensions. A standard 3-row, 5-reel ways-to-win slot has 3 possible row positions on each reel, and since a win just needs any matching symbol on each of the reels in sequence, the total number of possible winning combinations is 3 multiplied by itself once for each reel: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 243. Add a fourth row to each reel and that same math becomes 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 1,024, which is where the "1,024 ways" format comes from.

Grid shapeRows per reelReelsTotal ways
Standard 243-ways3535 = 243
1,024-ways4545 = 1,024
117,649-ways (6 rows)7676 = 117,649

Some developers push this further with variable-height reels — a reel might show two symbols on one spin and six on the next — which produces a constantly shifting ways total rather than a fixed number. Games built this way often market themselves as having "up to" a large maximum ways count rather than a single fixed figure, since the actual number changes spin to spin based on how tall each reel happens to be.

A worked example: the same reels, two different rulebooks

Picture a 5-reel, 3-row grid where the same cherry symbol happens to land on the top row of reel one, the bottom row of reel two, and the middle row of reel three, with no matching symbol on reels four or five.

  • On a 25-line payline slot: unless one specific active payline happens to zigzag through exactly top-bottom-middle across those first three reels, this pattern pays nothing at all — the cherries simply aren't aligned with any of the game's predefined paths.
  • On a 243-ways slot: this is an automatic three-of-a-kind win, because the cherries appear somewhere on each of the first three reels in sequence. The specific row each one lands in is irrelevant.

This is the central, practical difference between the two formats, and it's also why a ways-to-win slot's hit frequency — how often a spin returns any win at all, even a small one — tends to run noticeably higher than a comparable payline game built around the same base symbols and paytable.

What this means for hit frequency and bet sizing

Because a ways-to-win format counts more of the symbol arrangements that already land on the reels as winners, it naturally produces a higher hit frequency than an equivalent payline game. That doesn't automatically make it a better or worse bet in the long run — a game's designers set the actual payout amounts and reel weighting to land on whatever overall return to player (RTP) they're targeting regardless of format, a topic covered in full in our guide to understanding RTP. What changes is the texture of play: more frequent small wins with a ways format, versus longer stretches of nothing punctuated by less frequent wins on a traditional payline game with a similar RTP. Neither pattern is inherently better; it's a volatility and pacing question as much as anything else, which our slot volatility guide covers in more depth.

One wrinkle worth knowing: ways-to-win slots are almost always "all-ways active," meaning you're automatically betting on every one of the 243 (or however many) combinations with a single wager, rather than choosing how many lines to activate the way some older payline games allow. That simplifies betting, but it also means your total bet per spin is usually a flat multiple of a base unit rather than something you can trim down line by line.

Does RTP work any differently between the two?

No — RTP is calculated the same underlying way regardless of format: it's the long-run percentage of all money wagered that a game returns to players across its full mathematical cycle, derived from the weighted odds of every possible outcome and its associated payout. A 243-ways slot and a 25-line payline slot can both be built to a 96% RTP; the format doesn't set that number, the designer's paytable and reel-weighting choices do. What format does influence is how that return gets distributed across outcomes — more frequent, smaller contributions toward the total in a ways-to-win game, versus a mix shaped by whichever specific lines happen to be active in a payline game.

Fixed paylineWays-to-win
Win conditionMatching symbols on a predefined lineMatching symbols anywhere, reels left to right
Typical hit frequencyLower, all else equalHigher, all else equal
Betting structureOften adjustable number of active linesUsually all ways active by default
RTP determined byPaytable + reel weighting, same as any slotPaytable + reel weighting, same as any slot

How to tell which kind of slot you're actually playing

Every regulated online slot discloses its win structure in the in-game paytable or rules screen, usually right at the top — look for either a specific number of paylines (such as "25 lines") or an explicit "ways to win" figure (such as "243 ways" or "1,024 ways"). Games using variable-height reels typically state a maximum ways figure along with a note that the actual count changes spin to spin. If you're not sure which format a game you're trying is using, that paytable screen is the fastest way to find out — and it's worth a quick look before you start betting anyway, since it's also where the game discloses its specific RTP, volatility rating, and any bonus feature mechanics that affect how your money's actually being put at risk.

Frequently asked questions

Is a ways-to-win slot a better bet than a fixed payline slot?

Not inherently — the win-counting format doesn't set a game's RTP, the paytable and reel weighting do. A ways-to-win game will usually hit more often, but a payline game can be built with an equal or higher RTP depending on how its designer sized the payouts.

Why do some slots advertise "up to 1,024 ways" instead of a fixed number?

Those games use variable-height reels, where the number of visible symbol positions on each reel can change from spin to spin. Since the total ways count is the product of each reel's row count, a changing reel height means a changing ways total, so the game states its maximum rather than one fixed figure.

Can I choose how many paylines or ways to activate?

On most modern ways-to-win slots, no — all ways are active by default and your bet is a flat multiple of a base unit. Some older or classic-style payline slots do let you select fewer than the maximum number of lines, though doing so also reduces your chances of landing any given winning pattern.

Does a cluster-pay or Megaways slot use the same math as 243-ways?

They're related but distinct. Cluster-pay games count wins by groups of adjacent matching symbols touching in any direction rather than left-to-right reel sequences, and Megaways-style games combine variable reel heights with the same left-to-right ways logic described here, just scaled up to a much larger maximum. Our guide to Megaways and cluster-pay math breaks those two down separately.

Where do I find a specific game's exact ways-to-win count?

It's disclosed in the game's own paytable or rules screen, usually accessible from an info or menu icon in the game's interface, alongside its RTP and volatility rating.
